categorically prohibits muting any portion of BWC audio. lon interpreted the
statute to require the release of unedited video and audio recordings of an incident while permitting
 limited blurring to protect privacy, and it prohibited muting audio absent statutory authority.

Specifically,  the Court concluded  that BWC footage depicting a juvenile’s  fatal
 shooting could be released without muting the juvenile’s “gasps for breath and expression of pain,”
 explaining  that the audio portion revealed “the physical act of dying” and “the statute clearly
 contemplates the release of BWC video and audio recordings that depict death of an individual.”

Thus, the Court found  that  it could “discern no substantial privacy  interest that could be
 compromised by the release of the audio from the BWC footage.”

Notably, however, lon
 expressly declined to decide whether audio may be muted under other circumstances  to protect

 privacy  interests.

groups.proposition:
Where a statute announces a general rule of access
and carves out exceptions, the exceptions are narrowly construed and the party claiming one
carries the burden of bringing its record within it.

occurrences.proposition:
Where a statute announces a general rule of access
and carves out exceptions, the exceptions are narrowly construed and the party claiming one
carries the burden of bringing its record within it.

That principle, applied here, means
that the public-interest inquiry under the CCJRA is a conﬁned inquiry and not a general license
to weigh the reputational or institutional discomfort of the agency that holds the ﬁle. C.R.S. s
24-72-301;

The allocation is the settled construction of
Colorado's access statutes: the right of inspection is the general rule, the exemptions are
exceptions to it, and the party resisting disclosure must prove that the record falls within the
exception it claims.

Because the Act states a general rule of access and a discrete set of
exceptions, the exceptions are read no more broadly than their terms require, and a court does
not enlarge an exception by analogy, by implication, or by its own view of what the legislature
would have preferred.

opposing party's ability to prepare a defense to the amendment, most often when the amended

claims arise from a different subject matter and raise significant new factual issues.

The Tenth Circuit applies Rule 15(a)(2) to provide litigants the maximum opportunity for

each claim to be decided on the merits rather than on procedural technicalities.

Lateness alone does not justify denial of

amendment, but the Tenth Circuit focuses primarily on the reasons for delay and has held that



                                    Page 3 of 9Case No. 1:25-cv-02263-RMR-MDB  Document 84    filed 07/02/26  USDC Colorado
                                pg 4 of 9





denial may be appropriate when the moving party has no adequate explanation for delay.
The most important factor is whether the amendment would prejudice the opposing party.

Courts typically find prejudice only when the amendment unfairly affects the

opposing party's ability to prepare a defense to the amendment, most often when the amended

claims arise from a different subject matter and raise significant new factual issues.

occurrences.proposition:
categorically prohibits muting any portion of BWC audio. lon interpreted the
statute to require the release of unedited video and audio recordings of an incident while permitting
 limited blurring to protect privacy, and it prohibited muting audio absent statutory authority.

Specifically,  the Court concluded  that BWC footage depicting a juvenile’s  fatal
 shooting could be released without muting the juvenile’s “gasps for breath and expression of pain,”
 explaining  that the audio portion revealed “the physical act of dying” and “the statute clearly
 contemplates the release of BWC video and audio recordings that depict death of an individual.”

Thus, the Court found  that  it could “discern no substantial privacy  interest that could be
 compromised by the release of the audio from the BWC footage.”

Notably, however, lon
 expressly declined to decide whether audio may be muted under other circumstances  to protect

 privacy  interests.

groups.proposition:
The Ninth Circuit recognizes

four narrow circumstances in which private conduct may be treated as state action:

when the private party performs a function traditionally and exclusively reserved to

the State; when the State is a willful participant in joint activity with the private

actor; when the State has coerced or significantly encouraged the private conduct;

or when there is such a close nexus between the State and the challenged action

that the private conduct may be fairly treated as that of the State itself.

a

complaint need only contain “sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief

that is plausible on its face.’”

A claim is facially plausible when the plaintiff

pleads factual content that “allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant

is liable for the misconduct alleged.”

This standard is not a “probability requirement,” but it

asks for “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully.”

The Court’s inquiry is a “context-specific task that requires the reviewing court to draw

on its judicial experience and common sense.”

groups.proposition:
The Ninth Circuit recognizes

four narrow circumstances in which private conduct may be treated as state action:

when the private party performs a function traditionally and exclusively reserved to

the State; when the State is a willful participant in joint activity with the private

actor; when the State has coerced or significantly encouraged the private conduct;

or when there is such a close nexus between the State and the challenged action

that the private conduct may be fairly treated as that of the State itself.

redactions can be made."

argument, holding the provision limited by its own terms to records "requested

pursuant to this part 3," while an Integrity Act request is made under different

authority.

25     The division then stated the operative rule: an agency receiving a request for

a recording "will always have to make a threshold determination as to whether the

request is under the Integrity Act or the CCJRA to determine, among other things,

the applicable deadline for fulfilling the request and what, if any, redactions can be

made."
and 24-72-305(5) had no application to it.

Boulder

"advocate[d] for importing the CCJRA's enforcement provisions — which allow

appeals of a custodian's discretionary denial of access to records — into the

Integrity Act." The division answered: "these are policy arguments that should be

directed at the General Assembly, not this court."

There, Yellow Scene sought mandamus and declaratory relief over

Boulder's attempt to apply a CCJRA fee rule to an Integrity Act request.

The district court held an expedited hearing and entered

declaratory judgment defining the parties' rights.

This Court held that

"the district court did not err by entering declaratory relief."

and-talk, it is clearly established that officers are limited to “knock[ing] promptly, wait[ing]

briefly to be received, and then (absent invitation to linger longer) leav[ing].”

                                22       status.
